region.text: the Banten trading post, the first permanent Dutch post in Indonesia (1603)

ledger.note: 1602: the Dutch East India Company is established. 'Established on 20 March 1602' (article body and infobox); 'the first permanent Dutch trading post in Indonesia was established in Banten, West Java' (dated 1603 in the text). The company holds no land in 1602; the Banten post stands for the core.

region.text: Ambon island, taken from the Portuguese in 1605

ledger.note: 1605: the Dutch take Ambon. 'Amboina was captured from the Portuguese in 1605.' (VOC page: 'Dutch control of Ambon was achieved when the Portuguese surrendered their fort in Ambon to the Dutch-Hituese alliance', undated.)

region.text: the Banda Islands (Lontor and neighbours), invaded in 1621

ledger.note: 1609: the war for the Banda Islands begins. The page: 'the Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands, between 1609 and 1621, after the islands resisted the nutmeg monopoly'.

region.text: Jayakarta, stormed on 30 May 1619 and renamed Batavia

ledger.note: 30 May 1619: Coen takes Jayakarta. 'On 30 May 1619, Coen, backed by a force of nineteen ships, stormed Jayakarta, driving out the Banten forces'; the Dutch-Portuguese War page adds 'Batavia, conquered by Jan Pieterszoon Coen in 1619'.

1619: the seat moves from Ambon to Batavia. 'the VOC established a capital in the port city of Jayakarta in 1619 and changed its name to Batavia'; Ambon had housed the headquarters 'during the tenures of the first three governors-general (1610-1619)'.

region.text: the Banda Islands (Lontor and neighbours), invaded in 1621

ledger.note: 1621: the Banda conquest ends. 'They invaded the main Bandanese island of Lontor in 1621' (the conquest ran 'between 1609 and 1621').

region.text: the Banda Islands (Lontor and neighbours), invaded in 1621

ledger.note: 1621: the Banda Islands become Dutch. The page dates the conquest 'between 1609 and 1621' and the invasion of Lontor to 1621; the year of completion is read from that.

region.text: Makassar and Gowa

ledger.note: 24 November 1666: the Makassar War begins. The page: the war 'lasted from 24 November 1666 to 24 June 1669'; the Bongaya page adds that the VOC declared war on Gowa on 5 October 1666.

region.text: Jum Pandan, the stronghold converted into Fort Rotterdam

ledger.note: 18 November 1667: Gowa cedes Jum Pandan. 'Jum Pandan, a stronghold that would be converted into Fort Rotterdam, was ceded to the Dutch' (Bongaya page, signed 18 November 1667); the Makassar War page: Speelman built Fort Rotterdam 'as the headquarters of VOC activities in Sulawesi'. The place is read as Makassar's fort.

region.text: Minahasa, one of 'Gowa's dependencies' transferred to the Netherlands

ledger.note: 18 November 1667: Minahasa is transferred. The Bongaya page states: 'Gowa's dependicies, such as Minahasa, were transferred to the Netherlands'; the page does not say what the VOC held there in practice, and the radius is a reading.

region.text: Gowa's Cliopatria outline of 1662-1669

ledger.note: 18 November 1667: Gowa becomes a VOC vassal. 'Gowa was reduced to a vassal of the VOC.'

region.text: Makassar and Gowa

ledger.note: 24 June 1669: the Makassar War ends. 'lasted from 24 November 1666 to 24 June 1669'; 'Assault of Somba Opu began on 14 June 1669' and 'the Makassar forces had fled and abandoned Somba Opu'. Bone replaced Gowa as the supreme principality, 'with Palakka dominating internal affairs and the VOC dominating external affairs'.

minus.text: Cirebon, a Dutch protectorate from 1680 and ceded only in 1705

region.text: Bogor, Karawang and Priangan: West Java without the Cirebon area (handed over in 1680)

ledger.note: 1680: Mataram hands over West Java. 'Mataram has to hand over Bogor, Karawang and Priangan to the VOC' (Amangkurat II's accession, 1680). The page names the places; the West Java outline is the reading.

region.text: the region of Cirebon, ceded by Mataram in 1705

ledger.note: 1680: Cirebon becomes a Dutch protectorate. 'Cirebon too was forced to shift allegiance from Mataram to the Dutch, and becomes Dutch's protectorate state.'

region.text: Banten, the sultanate's West Java core

ledger.note: 1682: the Dutch fleet intervenes at Banten. Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa returned in 1682 to seize power from his son; the Dutch 'saw an opportunity to gain control upon Banten politics', 'dispatching the Dutch fleet to rescue the trapped young Sultan' (the step itself is undated on the page); 'a war broke out between Batavia and Banten in the 1680s'.

region.text: Banten, the sultanate's West Java core

ledger.note: 1683: the Banten war ends in a protectorate. 'the old Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa was forced to surrender' (he died in Batavia in 1692); the infobox gives 'Client state of VOC: 1683'. The end year is the infobox's.

region.text: Banten, the sultanate's West Java core

ledger.note: 1683: Banten becomes a VOC client state. Infobox 'Client state of VOC: 1683' (and 'Client state of the Dutch Empire (1683-1813)'); the war made it 'a protectorate of the VOC' and the Dutch demanded 'the Dutch monopoly on pepper trade, and the right to establish a Dutch garrison in Banten'.

region.text: the region of Cirebon, ceded by Mataram in 1705

ledger.note: 1705: Pakubuwono I cedes Cirebon. 'In 1705 he agreed to cede the regions of Cirebon and eastern part of Madura'; the VOC also received 'Semarang as new headquarters', 'the right to build fortresses anywhere in Java', and the opium, textile and rice rights.

region.text: the region of Cirebon, ceded by Mataram in 1705

ledger.note: 1705: the Cirebon protectorate becomes cession. The page: Cirebon was a Dutch protectorate from 1680 and was ceded to the VOC in 1705 (gain above).

region.text: the eastern part of Madura, ceded in 1705

ledger.note: 1705: eastern Madura. 'In 1705 he agreed to cede the regions of Cirebon and eastern part of Madura' (the article adds that Mataram had little real control there; the disc is a reading).

region.text: Semarang, given to the VOC in 1705 as its new headquarters

ledger.note: 1705: Semarang becomes the VOC's headquarters in Java. 'The VOC was given Semarang as new headquarters'; Amangkurat II had promised the town in 1677-78 ('He promised to give the VOC the port town of Semarang if they lend him some troops').

region.text: Surabaya, captured in 1718

ledger.note: 1718: Surabaya. 'The VOC managed to capture Surabaya after a bloody war in 1718.' The page does not name the loser (the Surabayan faction ended in Mataram in 1708); Mataram is given as counterpart.

region.text: the north coast of Java and Madura, ceded in 1743 (Giyanti page: 'ceded the north coast of Java and Madura to the Dutch East India Company')

ledger.note: 1743: the north coast and Madura. The Giyanti page: 'In 1743, the king ceded the north coast of Java and Madura to the Dutch East India Company'; Article 6 speaks of Madura and the coastal areas 'handed over in 1746', and the Mataram page: 'Susuhunan Pakubuwana II ceded sovereignty over the Pasisir to the VOC' (undated), 'by 1743 Mataram only consists of areas around Surakarta, Yogyakarta, Kedu and Bagelen'.

region.text: Mataram's last Cliopatria outline (1741-1743): the court lands around Surakarta, Yogyakarta, Kedu and Bagelen

ledger.note: 11 December 1749: Mataram is handed to the VOC. 'On 11 December 1749, Pakubuwana II signed an agreement in which the "sovereignty" of Mataram was given to the VOC'; infobox 'From 1749 onto 1755, Sultanate of Mataram is a Vassal of Dutch East India Company'.

region.text: southern Sumatra, 'territories on western Borneo and southern Sumatra formerly held by Banten' (1752)

ledger.note: 1752: Banten's outer lands. 'In 1752, the Dutch annexed territories on western Borneo and southern Sumatra formerly held by Banten.' Only the Sumatran part is drawn (Lampung, read from the page's 'southern Sumatra'); the page names no Bornean place.

region.text: Mataram's last Cliopatria outline

ledger.note: 13 February 1755: Mataram is divided. The Giyanti treaty was 'signed and ratified on February 13, 1755'; the eastern half went to Pakubuwono III at Surakarta and the western half to Mangkubumi at Yogyakarta (Mataram page: 'The kingdom of Mataram was divided in 1755').

region.text: Surakarta's Cliopatria outline

ledger.note: 13 February 1755: Surakarta under the VOC. The Giyanti page speaks of the company sending 'troops to assist its vassal king' (Pakubuwono III) and gives the VOC approval over appointments of the Dalem and regents and an oath of allegiance (Articles 3-4).

region.text: Yogyakarta's Cliopatria outline

ledger.note: 13 February 1755: Yogyakarta under the VOC. Mangkubumi, 'known as Sultan Hamengkubuwono I', took the western half; the page gives the VOC approval over appointments of the Dalem and regents (Articles 3-4), an oath of allegiance and fixed deliveries (Article 8). The page never uses the word vassal for Yogyakarta, hence confidence 2.

wars.name: Dutch-Portuguese War

zones.text: Ambon island, taken from the Portuguese in 1605

wars.outcome: Ambon fell in 1605, Batavia was taken in 1619, Malacca in 1641 (dutch-malacca dossier); the page says that in 1661 'Portugal agreed to compensate the Dutch with eight million guilders' and ceded Ceylon and the Maluku Islands.
wars.note: The page extract gives events from 1605 to 1661, not the war's own span; from/to are the first and last dated events read. Ceylon, Formosa and Cochin belong to other dossiers.

wars.name: Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands

zones.text: the Banda Islands (Lontor and neighbours), invaded in 1621

wars.outcome: 'the Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands, between 1609 and 1621, after the islands resisted the nutmeg monopoly'; Lontor was invaded in 1621.

wars.name: Makassar War
wars.outcome: VOC victory: Treaty of Bongaya (18 November 1667) ceded Jum Pandan (Fort Rotterdam) and Minahasa and made Gowa a vassal; Somba Opu fell in June 1669 and Bone, under Arung Palakka, replaced Gowa as the leading principality.
wars.note: The page: 'lasted from 24 November 1666 to 24 June 1669'.

wars.name: Dutch intervention in Banten
wars.outcome: Sultan Haji kept the throne with Dutch help against Ageng Tirtayasa, who surrendered; Banten became a VOC client state (1683).
wars.note: The page dates the crisis to 1682, the war loosely to 'the 1680s' and the client state to 1683.

certainty.note: Holdings are forts, ports and ceded districts named in the pages; none of the pages draws a boundary. The 1705 and 1743 Java cessions are the only block cessions with a stated extent (Cirebon, the north coast, Madura); even they were administrative claims over land the Company did not rule directly.

notes: Written 2026-10-24 by the se-03-x additions batch. A colony-type dossier for the Dutch East India Company's land in the Indonesian archipelago, 1602-1799, a state Cliopatria lacks as such. Seven pages opened (above the 2-5 budget: the company is the largest missing state of the group; the first three were needed for acquisitions, the last two for Java). COORDINATION: Cliopatria's Dutch Republic row (1582-1795) already draws Indonesian, Sri Lankan and Taiwanese cells (its 1609-1618 shapes reach 128E, the 1640+ shapes -20S); the eu-09 review of that row should drop the overseas cells so this dossier and dutch-malacca are not drawn twice. SCOPE: only the Indonesian archipelago is drawn here. Malacca (1641-1795) has its own dossier (dutch-malacca). Not drawn and without a dossier: Dutch Ceylon (VOC page: 'Dutch Ceylon from 1640 to 1796'; Galle 1640 and Colombo 1656 are named by the Dutch-Portuguese War page, which does not date Galle), Dutch Malabar ('from 1661 to 1795'), Dutch Formosa (Tayouan 1624, northern Formosa from Spain 1642, lost to Koxinga in 1662), the Cape ('between 1652 and 1806'; dutch-cape-colony exists), Mauritius, Coromandel, Suratte, Hirado/Dejima, Ayutthaya, Hanoi and Hoi An factories (VOC page). NOT ON THE PAGES: VOC suzerainty over Ternate, Tidore, Bacan, Bima, Jambi, Palembang, Johor and Sumbawa, the Moluccas treaties, Timor (Kupang; the page says only that 'Dutch advances were halted by an autonomous and powerful group of Portuguese Eurasians called the Topasses'), the west Sumatra coast (the page gives only the 1663 Painan Treaty with 'several local lords in the Painan area'), the Third Javanese War of Succession, the British seizure of Malacca (January 1795, in the Dutch Malacca page), Ceylon (1796), Ambon and Banda (1796) and Padang (1795). The 1795-1799 holdings are therefore drawn as unchanged to 31 December 1799, which is wrong for Ambon and Banda if the British seized them in 1796 (not on the pages). VASSALS: the suzerain's convention is followed (counterpart = the vassal). Sibling dossiers (sultan-of-yogyakarta, surakarta-sunanate) record the 1755-1799 suzerain as dutch-republic; this dossier carries the mirror pair and the orchestrator should reconcile the counterpart strings. Mataram's own dossier should carry the 1749-1755 vassalage. PAGE CONFLICTS: the Mataram page dates the Pasisir cession only by context, the Giyanti page says 1743 and also speaks of Madura and the coast 'handed over in 1746'; 1743 is used. The Mataram page promises Semarang in 1677-78 and gives it in 1705. Minahasa as a Gowa dependency is the Bongaya page's claim and is unverified elsewhere.
